metadata.title: Combination of Entner-Doudoroff pathway with MEP increases isoprene production in engineered Escherichia coli

reference.title: Combination of Entner-Doudoroff pathway with MEP increases isoprene production in engineered Escherichia coli

engineering_problem.problem_statement: Isoprene production in engineered E. coli is limited by precursor imbalance in the MEP (2-C-methyl-D-erythritol 4-phosphate) pathway rather than by terminal pathway enzyme capacity alone.
trigger_conditions: target product depends on the MEP (isoprenoid) pathway
terminal pathway enzyme overexpression alone has not achieved the desired titer
an alternative central-metabolism route (e.g. Entner-Doudoroff pathway) is available to rewire precursor supply

observations: increasing terminal MEP-pathway enzyme expression alone does not proportionally increase isoprene titer
MEP-pathway flux depends on precursor ratios (e.g. pyruvate and glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate) supplied by central carbon metabolism
bottlenecks: imbalanced ratio of MEP-pathway precursors from central carbon metabolism
over-reliance on terminal-enzyme overexpression without addressing upstream precursor supply
biological_diagnosis.mechanistic_explanation: The MEP pathway that produces isoprene depends on precursors generated by central carbon metabolism; if the ratio of those precursors is unbalanced, increasing terminal MEP-pathway enzyme levels does not proportionally raise flux, because the pathway remains supply-limited rather than capacity-limited.

engineering_hypothesis.hypothesis: Combining an alternative central-metabolism route (Entner-Doudoroff pathway) with the native route rebalances MEP-pathway precursor ratios, increasing carbon flux to isoprene beyond what terminal-enzyme overexpression alone achieves.
engineering_hypothesis.expected_effect: improved and better-balanced precursor supply to the MEP pathway, raising isoprene titer/yield

engineering_actions.target: central carbon metabolism precursor supply (e.g. pyruvate, glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate) for the MEP pathway
engineering_actions.gene_or_pathway: Entner-Doudoroff pathway (combined with the native route); specific gene identities are not specified in the problem summary available to this V1 knowledge base and require review of the primary text
engineering_actions.source: Liu et al., "Combination of Entner-Doudoroff pathway with MEP increases isoprene production in engineered Escherichia coli" (journal/year/DOI not provided in the source summary available to this V1 knowledge base)
engineering_actions.rationale: the core finding is that precursor ratio optimization and central-metabolism rewiring, not terminal-enzyme overexpression alone, is the key lever for relieving the MEP-pathway bottleneck.
engineering_actions.expected_effect: improved balance of MEP-pathway precursors supporting higher isoprene flux
engineering_actions.risk: rewiring central carbon metabolism can affect growth and other biosynthetic pathways that share the same precursor pools
validation: measure intracellular pyruvate/G3P pool ratios before and after rewiring
compare isoprene titer with and without central-metabolism rewiring
confirm via enzyme-activity assays that terminal MEP-pathway enzymes are not the sole bottleneck

engineering_actions.gene_or_pathway: MEP pathway terminal genes; specific gene identities are not specified in the problem summary available to this V1 knowledge base
engineering_actions.source: Liu et al., "Combination of Entner-Doudoroff pathway with MEP increases isoprene production in engineered Escherichia coli" (journal/year/DOI not provided in the source summary available to this V1 knowledge base)
engineering_actions.rationale: terminal-enzyme overexpression remains useful, but per the core rule it should be a secondary step after precursor supply is addressed, not the sole strategy.
engineering_actions.expected_effect: additional flux increase once precursor imbalance has been relieved
engineering_actions.risk: overexpressing terminal enzymes without addressing precursor supply adds metabolic burden without proportional yield gain
validation: compare isoprene titer from terminal-enzyme overexpression alone versus combined with precursor rebalancing

decision_rules.condition: terminal pathway enzymes have been overexpressed but titer improvement plateaus
decision_rules.recommended_strategy: check precursor pool balance in central carbon metabolism before further terminal-enzyme engineering
decision_rules.reason: unbalanced precursor ratios cap flux regardless of terminal enzyme levels

decision_rules.condition: an alternative central-metabolism route is available (e.g. Entner-Doudoroff pathway)
decision_rules.recommended_strategy: combine the alternative route with the native precursor-generating pathway to rebalance flux
decision_rules.reason: this addresses precursor imbalance directly rather than relying solely on downstream enzyme expression

decision_rules.recommended_strategy: do not rely on increasing terminal enzymes alone; rewire central metabolism when necessary
decision_rules.reason: terminal-enzyme-only strategies leave the upstream precursor-supply bottleneck unaddressed

generalizable_rules: when a product depends on a precursor pool shared with central metabolism, diagnose precursor balance before increasing terminal pathway enzyme expression
rewiring central carbon metabolism, not only terminal pathway enzymes, is sometimes necessary to relieve precursor-driven bottlenecks
